svg.title: Module 03 one-page guide: The Anatomy of an Agent
svg.text: CSCI 391 · MODULE 03 · ONE-PAGE LECTURE GUIDE
The Anatomy of an Agent
Five parts — not four, not six: model, tools, memory, loop, termination policy.
Part I · Foundations and Mindset · Week 3 · Read: Caldwell, The Agentic AI Bible, Ch. 3
OPENING CASE
Remember the refund agent? It invented a refund policy instead of telling the customer it wasn't confident. It was
missing an organ: the termination check that would have forced it to say “I don't know” before anything else.
It's easy to program something that looks like an agent but is missing a
critical part. The termination policy is the one most often left out.
KEY FRAMEWORK
Five-part anatomy
Model — does the reasoning and emits tool calls
Tool set — what the agent can do in the world
Memory — at minimum a rolling context window
Loop — alternates deliberation and action
Termination policy — knows when to stop
YOU SHOULD BE ABLE TO
Identify the five essential components of an agent
Explain how each component fails and what that
failure looks like
Make agent runs reproducible: pinned versions,
logged seeds, captured traces
Implement a bounded ordering agent (Coffee Shop
Agent)
ENTERPRISE LENS · ADDISON BOYER
Production systems pin model versions, log seeds, and keep traces of the exact messages sent. If you can't replay
a run, you can't debug it.
Make the termination policy code, not prose: max steps, max spend, wall-clock limit, and an explicit 'cannot
complete' exit.
In code review, I look for the loop's exit conditions first. They tell me more about an agent's safety than its
prompt does.
I've watched a model call a one-argument calculator tool with two invented operands. Validate inputs before
executing, and return typed errors (a success flag plus “customer email must be a valid email address”), never a
raw stack trace.
DISCUSS
→ Which component is most often mistaken for the entire agent?
→ What does a termination policy look like for an agent with no natural 'done' state?
Concepts after Caldwell, The Agentic AI Bible, Ch. 3. Case framing, synthesis, and enterprise lens: Addison Boyer.
